newsitem.title: USA: YEAREND - High-yield credits seen stalwarts in '97.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - High-yield credits seen stalwarts in '97.

text.p: Improving credit profiles of high-yield issuers and better liquidity should underpin fundamentals in the high-yield debt market for 1997 and keep defaults near historical lows, analysts said.

Even cyclical businesses should be able to weather upcoming troughs thanks to yield-hungry investors and favorable refinancing environment, some said. What's more, some analysts said high-yielders will glean support via the powerful performance of U.S. equities.

"I really don't see a rise in default rates in 1997," said David Unger, a managing director of First Chicago Capital Markets Inc's high-yield group. "With the equity market remaining strong, there is better support, better capitalization for companies in the high-yield market."

Many analysts opined there will be some worsening, but that is coming off a default rate that fell from month to month in 1996. Moody's Investors Services' trailing 12-months default rate, based on the percentage of issuers, fell from a high of 3.47 in January to 1.62 in November.
The 25-year average rate of defaults is around 3.5 percent.

On the buyside, Christopher Molumphy, senior portfolio manager of the $2.3 billion Franklin Age High-Income Fund, also expects a fiscally sound year for most companies based on a sanguine outlook of the U.S. economy. But the rate itself will likely post a non-threatening rise next year, he said.
"Since we are getting gradually later in the cycle I would expect (defaults) to edge up a bit in 1997," Molumphy said, adding that he would "certainly expect them to be below longer-term averages."

Looking specifically at commodity-type businesses, Unger said those businesses are better equipped to handle cyclical downturns. Companies like Stone Container Corp that had been facing bankruptcy when prices hit lows two to three years ago should survive, he said, because interest coverages are stronger now and maturity profiles have been extended.
Molumphy added the rate of cyclical business growth during the current upswing has been less than typical, and any recession (or rise in defaults) should therefore be less severe.

This is not to say high-yielders won't meet with tough times when it comes time to pay the piper, however. Many companies may have dodged the bullet thanks to a forgiving credit environment in 1996, said Martin Fridson, global high-yield strategist at Merrill Lynch & Co Inc.

"We think this market is the flip side of 1990 where you had a credit crunch and companies that should have made it did not because banks were not in the position to extend any more forebearance and now you have the exact opposite," Fridson said. "There's so much liquidity sloshing around that companies that shouldn't make it do."

There is some correlation between an increase in lower-tier issuance and a rising default rate, Fridson said. However, he said voluminous issuance of the early to mid-1990s has yet to result in a significant rise in defaults thanks to current liquidity conditions.
In any event, the relationship between heavier issuance and default rates would be a lagging one because companies tend to finance at the top of their business cycles, he said.

At the same time, Fridson noted the business cycle is perhaps not the best barometer of defaults. The severe recession of 1982 fostered a default rate around 4.0 percent, he said, while they hit record high levels in the milder recession of the early 1990s.

Fitch Investors Service Director Randy Szuch and Assistant Director Kevin Lydon also suggested the market's heady liquidity will buffer the environment for potentially troubled credits. But that very liquidity should also spawn an air of caution for fixed-income investors as the end of the business cycle uptrend nears, Szuch said.
The structure of bank loans is perhaps not as tight as it should be, they said.
"The covenants are weakening," Lydon said. "We're seeing an increased supply of cash and therefore the syndicates don't have the incentive to make these structures very tight."
The Fitch analysts study bank loans, which generally fall into the single-B and BB asset classes.

Molumphy has subscribed to a cautiously optimistic view for high-yielders and the economy for 1997. That translates into a continuation of the more conservative strategy adopted by the Age Fund in 1996, he said.

Growth-oriented sectors, such as media and telecommunications, are long-term favorites for Molumphy. Conversely, he said cyclicals such as paper, forest products and retailers may not offer enough return for the risk as the business cycle's upswing ages.
First Chicago's Unger recommends a credit specific approach to investing in 1997 instead of making sector bets.
-- U.S. Corporate Bond Unit, 212-859-1672
